Young-of-year Blunthead cichlids emerge from the egg at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0011 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0011 grams]. This minute initial mass, comparable to that of a small grain of sand, reflects the pelagic, yolk-dependent stage of the newly hatched prolarva. As the yolk-sac is progressively absorbed and the mouth opens, these larvae initiate exogenous feeding and begin a period of rapid growth. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], individuals in aquaria have been observed to reach the onset of gonadal activation at a modest total length of 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters]. This measurement represents the total length at puberty, a point at which the sub-adult fish begins the hormonal cascade leading to vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. The relatively small size at maturation is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive activity, a common trait among rock-dwelling cichlids from Lake Tanganyika where territory acquisition is a key selective pressure.

Once sexual maturation is achieved, a female Tropheus moorii is capable of producing a single clutch of fertilized eggs after each mouthbrooding cycle. The maximum reproductive rate under these conditions, observed at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], corresponds to a typical clutch size of approximately 5 to 15 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 5 to 15 eggs per spawning event] and an inter-spawning interval of roughly 3 to 4 weeks during the peak breeding season, yielding approximately 12 to 17 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 12 to 17 spawning events per year]. This brooding female carries the developing embryos and later the yolk-sac larvae in her buccal cavity for an extended period, during which she does not feed. This mouthbrooding strategy imposes a significant energetic cost, limiting the annual reproductive output compared to substrate-spawning cichlids. The thermal regime of 25 °C appears to be near the optimal range for both gonadal recrudescence and larval development in this species, as deviations from this temperature can suppress spawning frequency or increase the duration of the buccal incubation phase.

As individuals progress through the juvenile phase, their body mass increases substantially from the initial hatchling value. The ultimate wet weight of a fully-grown adult Blunthead cichlid has been estimated at 42.6 grams [Wwi = 42.6 grams], derived from length-weight relationships typical of the species. This adult body mass is attained when the fish reaches its maximum recorded total length of 14.5 centimeters [Li = 14.5 centimeters]. The relationship between length and weight in Tropheus moorii follows a strongly positive allometric scaling, reflecting the deep-bodied, laterally compressed morphology characteristic of the genus. Older, dominant males in stable social hierarchies often approach this asymptotic size, while females tend to remain slightly smaller on average. In comparison to its congener Tropheus duboisi, which can reach a slightly larger maximum size, the ultimate total length of 14.5 centimeters [Li = 14.5 centimeters] for Tropheus moorii positions it as a medium-sized inhabitant of the rocky littoral zone. Reaching this size requires several years of continuous growth, contingent upon consistent access to the filamentous algae and aufwuchs that constitute its primary diet.

At the onset of reproductive maturity, a female Blunthead cichlid typically weighs around 3 grams [Wwp = around 3 grams], which is the wet weight at puberty corresponding to the total length of 6 centimeters. This body mass represents a critical threshold, as it indicates that the fish has accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support the demanding process of mouthbrooding. After this point, growth continues but at a decelerated rate, as more resources are channeled into gametogenesis and parental care. The gonadosomatic index rises sharply once this size is surpassed, with females producing clutches of 5 to 15 fully yolked oocytes. Intraspecific variation in the size at puberty is low in wild populations of Tropheus moorii from the Kigoma region, likely due to the stabilizing selection imposed by intense competition for algal grazing territories. In captivity, slight differences in diet quality can advance or delay the age at which a sub-adult reaches this 3-gram body mass (3 grams) [Wwp = 3 grams], but the total length of 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters] remains a remarkably consistent predictor of reproductive activation across different lineages.

The maximum recorded lifespan of Tropheus moorii under natural conditions in Lake Tanganyika has been documented at approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a value that is remarkable among cichlids of at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]its size class. This longevity is likely facilitated by the species' conservative life-history strategy, slow growth after maturity, and the relatively stable thermal environment of the lake, which averages 25 °C [T = 25 °C] throughout the year in the upper water column. Senescent individuals show a gradual decline in body condition and a reduced frequency of spawning events during the final one to two years of life. In comparison, captive specimens maintained in aquaria with optimal water quality and reduced predation pressure have been known to survive for over a decade [am = over a decade], although they seldom exceed the 10-year mark (10 years) [am = 10 years] recorded in field studies at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The trade-off between this extended lifespan and the modest annual reproductive output, where each female produces only a handful of offspring per brood, underscores the equilibrium life-history of this endemic Tanganyikan cichlid. Physiological death in the wild is typically preceded by a period of reproductive senescence, marking the completion of a life cycle that spans nearly a full decade in the rocky shallows of the lake.
